extracted.intended_audience: aspiring poets, literary critics, and educated readers of literary theory
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for evaluating and producing poetry: criteria of diction, imagination, tone, and the moral/psychological traits of genius. Emphasizes natural diction, precision, re-readability, and the avoidance of certain stylistic vices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Re-readability / enduring pleasure
rubrics_metrics.description: “Not the poem which we have read, but that to which we return, with the greatest pleasure, possesses the genuine power and claims the name of essential poetry.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A true poem is judged by whether it repays repeated readings with renewed pleasure; immediate charm alone is insufficient. Prefer works that reward return visits over transient impressiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-interchangeability of diction (verbal necessity)
rubrics_metrics.description: “Lines can be translated into other words of the same language without diminution of their significance ... are so far vicious in their diction.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good poetic diction should be necessary and not replaceable by synonymous wording without loss. If wording can be freely paraphrased with no diminution, the diction is defective. Example/anti-pattern: phrases that mean the same when reworded show lack of precise phrasing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid pleasure from mere novelty or astonishment
rubrics_metrics.description: Exclude from 'worthy feelings' the pleasure derived from mere novelty in the reader, and the desire of exciting wonderment at his powers in the author.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Poetry aimed mainly to astonish or show off cleverness (novelty for novelty's sake) is not a high poetic aim. The poet should not seek applause by surprising tricks disconnected from deeper feeling or meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genuine admiration is an under-current, not ostentatious marks
rubrics_metrics.description: Genuine admiration is a continuous under-current of feeling; it is everywhere present, but seldom anywhere as a separate excitement—unlike the self-admiring 'marks' at line-ends seen in some French tragedy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid explicit rhetorical 'marks of admiration' (self-congratulatory signals) in verse. True greatness shows itself subtly and evenly rather than by emphatic flourishes that call attention to the poet's own cleverness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Precision and indivisibility of great poets' words
rubrics_metrics.description: It would be scarcely more difficult to push a stone out from the pyramids with the bare hand than to alter a word, or the position of a word, in Milton or Shakespeare ... without making the author say something else, or something worse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In great poetry each word/placement carries weight; careless alteration often degrades meaning. Evaluate wording precision and resist gratuitous edits; high-quality poems show near-indispensability of phrasing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Natural diction over affected/arbitrary language
rubrics_metrics.description: Praise for 'natural language, neither bookish nor vulgar' — elders (Donne to Cowley) had fantastic thoughts in pure mother English; moderns often have obvious thoughts in fantastic and arbitrary language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer language that feels organic and true to native idiom rather than artificially ornate or contrived 'poetic' diction. Anti-patterns include bookish archaisms or fantastical constructions that obscure sense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance heart and head (natural thought + natural diction)
rubrics_metrics.description: Bowles and Cowper were the first who combined natural thoughts with natural diction; the first who reconciled the heart with the head.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strong poetry unites genuine feeling (heart) with thoughtful intelligence (head) expressed in natural language. Avoid sacrificing passion to mere intellect (wit) or sacrificing both to surface ornament.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sin: doleful egotism and recurrence of favorite phrases
rubrics_metrics.description: One of the three sins of poetry: verse meant to excite a good-natured laugh at the spirit of doleful egotism and the recurrence of favourite phrases (self-obsessive mannerism).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid poems that center on self-pitying egotism or repeatedly recycle the author's favorite mannerisms; these produce triviality or ridicule rather than lasting art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sin: false/simple language that masks poor thought
rubrics_metrics.description: One of the three sins: low, creeping language and thoughts, under the pretence of simplicity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beware of adopting a spurious humility or 'simplicity' that conceals poverty of thought or craft. Simplicity should be genuine and earned, not a device to excuse weak imagination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sin: indiscriminate use of elaborate language and imagery
rubrics_metrics.description: One of the three sins: the indiscriminate use of elaborate and ameliorating language and imagery (overornamented style).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid gratuitous ornament and pomp of imagery that does not serve the poem's thought or feeling. Excessive, heterogeneous imagery can fragment meaning and degrade poetic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coherence: collective meaning over pleasing isolated images
rubrics_metrics.description: Critique of poets whose separate images and phrases give pleasure successively without a coherent collective meaning (example: certain lines of Pope vs. Spenser/Fletcher).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge poems by the unity of thought and the coherence of collective meaning, not merely by a succession of well-turned phrases or dazzling images that, together, make nonsense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetry demands sustained attention and delicate craft
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no profession which requires an attention so early, so long, or so unintermitting, as that of poetry; the mechanical task of verse is difficult and delicate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate poets by the depth of craft and sustained care in composition. The making of verse is a demanding craft; signs of hurried or careless manufacture are defects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sensibility as component of genius — oriented outward
rubrics_metrics.description: Sensibility, quick and deep, is a characteristic and a component part of genius; but true genius's sensibility is excited by causes beyond its own personal interests.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Genius shows deep feeling, but that feeling is primarily engaged by ideas, images, and the ideal world rather than by petty personal grievances. Self-centered sensitivity is not a mark of highest genius.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appeal to truth, nature, logic over mere authority
rubrics_metrics.description: No authority can avail in opposition to truth, nature, logic, and the laws of universal grammar; critical opinions should be grounded in faculties of the human mind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing style or poetry, prefer arguments from intrinsic truth, natural effect, and psychological/linguistic principles rather than citation of authorities. Use comparative examples (Greek, Chaucer, Milton) only to illustrate, not to override reasoned judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware mechanized, epigrammatic, commodity literature
rubrics_metrics.description: The mass diffusion of literature and mechanization of language produce a barrel-organ effect—epigrammatic periods that spare the reader thought and prevent intellectual effort.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value work that engages the reader intellectually rather than formulaic epigrams that imitate sense. High literature resists mechanized production and rewards effortful reading.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical reception: originality may diminish in contemporaries' eyes
rubrics_metrics.description: Original genius becomes less striking in proportion to its success in improving the taste and judgment of contemporaries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating a poet's impact, consider that success in shaping taste can make the poet's innovation seem less remarkable to later readers; apparent decline in strikingness can reflect improved taste, not loss of value.
